correctness.rationale: The exact equality H/J=sum_c binom(N_c,2)-m+b is valid for every configuration. Integer convexity minimizes the color-population term, parity forces at least one bicolored deleted pair in the two nonzero residue classes, and all equality cases are explicitly constructed and exhausted. Factorial counts, defect probabilities and Stirling asymptotics follow. Independent full-graph brute force at m=2..6 and pair-transfer checks at m=2..18 reproduced the formulas; finite tests are not substituted for the proof.

originality.rationale: The examined primary texts establish the general antiferromagnetic Potts framework, chromatic-polynomial zero-frustration results on different graphs, and ground-state entropy in lattice models. They do not derive the exact positive-frustration minimum and full split-pair ground-state count of the complete graph minus a perfect matching. The generic Potts partition function encodes finite energies abstractly but does not itself evaluate this family. Targeted graph, alias, exact count and implication searches found no stronger coverage, subject to unindexed-priority risk.
residual_risks: An earlier equivalent result may be indexed under maximum three-cut or minimum monochromatic edge count rather than the Potts name.
General graph-polynomial representations encode all spin energies in principle, and an unexamined special evaluation could cover these formulas.
The scanned primary sections do not amount to exhaustive inspection of all historical literature; originality is provisional pending independent review.

value.rationale: A natural three-state uniform antiferromagnet on the highly symmetric cross-polytope/cocktail-party graph has an exact nonzero-frustration ground-state classification for every m. The zero-vs-one split-pair coexistence in two residue classes, asymptotically almost-certain defect selection, and a different subexponential ground-state entropy prefactor in the third class are structural effects not supplied by simple zero-energy chromatic counts. They can inform finite-size statistical mechanics of dense multipartite frustration.
